title: History Dependence in Thermodynamic Properties of Solids

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Glass physics has been studied for over a century, yet a consistent understanding is still lacking [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. The nature of glass transition, Kauzmann’s paradox [ 8 ] are representative examples of this difficulty. The main problem lies in the difficulty of describing the nonequilibrium characters of glass. Numerous studies have therefore focused on these nonequilibrium aspects. In this line of research, the nonequilibrium characterization of glass is generally taken for granted. However, it is not obvious why glasses are considered nonequilibrium materials. Historically, the nonequilibrium characterization of glass emerged in discussions of the third law of thermodynamics. When the third law was discovered at the early twentieth century, the treatment of the residual entropy of glass became a subject of debate, because residual entropy appears to contradict the statement of the third law. This apparent contradiction led to extensive discussions [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ], which continue to this day [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 – 25 ] 1 . The generally-held explanation is that the current state of glass is not an equilibrium state but is instead evolving toward the equilibrium state, which may be the crystal phase [ 26 ,  27 ]. However, to date no evidence has been found indicating that silica glass crystallizes spontaneously. On the contrary, considerable evidence suggests that silica glass retains its amorphous state over extremely long timescales [ 7 ]. Glass artifacts produced in ancient times remain unchanged; natural glasses formed during the age of dinosaurs still exist in the glassy state; and lunar glass formed more than 3 billion years ago remain amorphous. In contrast, no metal can retain its original structure for one thousand years. This discrepancy reveals an inconsistency in how the concept of equilibrium is applied to glass and to ordinary materials.

Aside from the third law issue, the hysteresis of glass is a common reason for the nonequilibrium characterization of glass. 2  The current properties of a glass depend on the past history that the glass has undergone. However, closer observation indicates that hysteresis is a common property of solids. It is well known that the mechanical properties of steel are affected by previous thermal and mechanical treatments. It would not be an overstatement to say that the major subjects of metallurgy concern the hysteresis behaviors of solids. If hysteresis were regarded as an indicator of nonequilibrium, it would imply that no solids are in equilibrium.

The original motivation of this study is to clarify the equilibrium characterization of glass, which differs from the generally accepted view that glasses are in nonequilibrium states [ 36 ,  37 ]. This conclusion is obtained by examining the rigorous definition of state variables for solids, as indicated by Eq. ( 2 ) [ 34 ]. A free-energy argument unambiguously indicates that a glass is more stable than the parent liquid state [ 36 ]. As described above, the main reason for the traditional view of nonequilibrium characterization of glass is the history dependence of its properties. However, the author notes that there is no rigorous definition of hysteresis in the thermodynamics literature 4 . In fact, hysteresis describes a change in state, but a state cannot be specified without identifying the relevant state variables. Therefore, it is necessary to revisit the traditional view of the nonequilibrium characterization of glass from the perspective of thermodynamic description of hysteresis. This is the main purpose of the present paper. The glass issue may be too broad to be fully addressed in a single paper. To conclude definitively that the traditional view of nonequilibrium characterization of glass is incorrect, a comprehensive investigation would be required, including investigation on free energy [ 36 ,  38 ], specific heat [ 39 ,  40 ], phase transitions [ 37 ]. To avoid making the scope of the present study too broad, we restrict the discussion to the hysteresis issue. The reader should therefore note that the conclusion of this paper is derived solely from the investigation on hysteresis. For the consistency of the present conclusion with other properties, the reader is referred to the original papers [ 36 ,  37 ,  38 ,  39 – 40 ]. A review is now available [ 41 ], in which the origins of hysteresis in specific heat are described in detail from a microscopic perspective.

In Sect.  3 , the experimental facts of hysteresis in solids are analyzed. Hysteresis is observed in a wide range of solid properties, such as magnetic properties [ 42 ,  43 – 44 ], mechanical properties of metals [ 45 ,  46 – 47 ], and properties of glass [ 48 ,  49 ]. The subjects are too broad to be covered in this paper. Nonetheless, given the author’s background in materials research, a general thermodynamics investigation can be presented here. The treated examples are taken primarily from engineering research. This choice is motivated by the fact that, despite the prevalence of history-dependent phenomena in these areas, traditional thermodynamics studies do not highlight them enough. This situation reveals a significant gap between the fundamentals of thermodynamics and the engineering applications. Each application area employs different terminologies. The author therefore attempts to maintain consistent terminology throughout the paper; the relevant terms are explained at the beginning, in Sect.  2 . During analyzing various hysteresis phenomena in solids, readers may realize a circular problem in defining equilibrium and state variables. This problem is resolved in an axiomatic approach presented in Sect.  4 . There, starting from a rigorous definition of equilibrium, state variables are defined in a consistent manner. The arguments in this section are essentially the same as those in the author’s previous preprint [ 34 ]. However, because of the importance of the subject, the arguments are presented again here, with placing particular emphasis on the distinction between static states and slow processes. The present topics are so fundamental to thermodynamics that the study has many impacts on a wide range applications. Accordingly, the author has received a variety of questions and criticisms on different occasions. These questions are collected in a form of FAQ in Supplemental materials.

sections.heading: Assumptions and Definitions
paragraphs: Because this paper addresses very fundamental problems, the assumptions employed must be stated explicitly at the outset. Only the first and second laws of thermodynamics are assumed. Although these laws are well known, greater careful is required in their formulation in the present context. Some explanations are thus provided. In addition, definitions of several terms are given, because their usage differs across different fields.

sections.heading: Postulate 2.2

paragraphs: At the first glance, this formulation may appear somewhat unusual: why must the existence of equilibrium be assumed in stating the second law? It turns out that this statement is equivalent to the generally accepted maximum entropy principle, which asserts that a system attains the maximum of entropy at equilibrium (Ref. [ 52 ], p. 103). The maximum entropy principle was proposed more than a century ago by Gibbs [ 53 ]. He considered the general criterion for equilibrium and stated:

Gibbs’ criterion for equilibrium :  For the equilibrium of any isolated system it is necessary and sufficient that in all possible variations of the state of the system which do not alter its energy, the variation of its entropy shall either vanish or be negative.  (Ref. [ 53 ],p. 56)

In fact, this statement is equivalent to Postulate  2.2 . Hence, it may be used either as the statement of the second law or as the definition of equilibrium, provided entropy is already defined. However, readers may be aware of attachment of constraints in Postulate  2.2 , whereas no such condition appears in the Gibbs’ statement. This point is crucial to the present study and is fully discussed in Sect.  4 .

sections.heading: Structure
Stable, Metastable, and Frozen States
paragraphs: In the glass literature, the terms  frozen state  or  kinetically frozen state  are often used to refer to the glass state. The usual explanation is that, in glass-forming materials, the viscosity of the liquid becomes so high that atom motions effectively cease before the equilibrium state is reached. Some authors regard the frozen state as a metastable state, similar to state  b  in Fig.  2 . In this interpretation, frozen states do not differ from metastable state. Hence, some authors explain that the frozen state is even not metastable state but rather an unstable state such as  c  in figure (see Ref. [ 12 ], p. 61). In this picture, similar to a stone resting on a slope, the structure  c  is fixed due to the frictional force. However, the idea of frictional force does not exist at the fundamental level of quantum mechanics. Friction is not a fundamental interaction in microscopic mechanics. Rather, it is an effective description of energy dissipation that emerges when the dynamics of many degrees of freedom are coarse-grained: the energy initially assigned to a particular degree of freedom is redistributed among many degrees of freedoms in an uncontrollable manner. What actually impedes atomic motion is the presence of energy barriers. In the present work, frozen states are treated as metastable states. Terms such as megabasins or inherent structures are commonly used in the glass literature to describe these states. In the present context, all such states correspond to local minima in the potential energy landscape of the configurational space.

The former is a special case of the latter, when an external field  X  is varied in a cyclic manner. The main problem for glass is how to determine whether the initial state has truly been restored. sections.heading: Removal of Time Dependence from History Dependence
paragraphs: The approach of thermodynamics is to study the properties of a system through its static states. History dependence implies time dependence. By definition, a process describes time evolution and the state during a process is a nonequilibrium state. However, in the thermodynamic context, history dependence is not necessarily the same as time dependence. This point can be confusing, as explained in Sect.  2.1.1 . When we refer to the history dependence, we usually mean the effect of previous treatment on the current properties of a system after the treatment process has been completed. In most cases, the measurements of current properties are performed sufficiently long after the treatment, ensuing that the system has reached a static state. In short, a static state corresponds to an equilibrium state; this equivalence is discussed further in Sect.  4.2 . Typical experiments such as annealing or mechanical treatments fall into this category.

sections.heading: Separation of Thermal and Mechanical Relaxations
Phase Diagram
paragraphs: Diamond is perhaps the most well-known example that does not conform to the phase diagram. Diamond is one of the most stable material on Earth; yet, this phase does not occupy any temperature region in the phase diagram of carbon unless extreme high pressures, of the order of 1 GPa, are applied. At normal pressures, graphite is stable over the entire temperature range [ 66 ]. This example demonstrates that the stability of materials is rather governed by the energy barrier, as explained in II B c . In Fig.  2 , a metastable state  d  has a higher energy than  a , but the energy barrier surrounding  d  is larger than that around  a . The peculiarity of diamond extends beyond this point. Until the 1980s, it was believed that high-pressure methods were only means of synthesizing human-made diamond. Surprisingly, diamond can now be synthesized even at low pressures through plasma chemical-vapor deposition (CVD) method [ 67 ,  68 – 69 ]. The quality of the thin-film diamond synthesized by CVD is sufficiently high to enable heavily doping [ 70 ]. Because diamond is not the lowest-energy state at normal pressures, the mechanism must go beyond the Ostwald step rule. The involvement of hydrogen gas in plasma processes may play an active role in blocking the transition path to graphite: see [ 71 ] for a review. A phase diagram indicates how the equilibrium state changes with changing  T  and  V , but it does not imply that  T  and  V  are the only state variables for solids.

sections.heading: Equilibrium Concentration of Defects
paragraphs: The silicon crystals used in electronic devices are among the most perfect crystals produced by humans. Dislocation-free crystals have been achieved using a special technique [ 72 ]. Nevertheless, intrinsic point defects, such as vacancies and interstitials, still remain. Engineers working on Si wafers became more acutely aware of the presence of these intrinsic defects after dislocation-free crystals were achieved. Dislocations act as sinks that trap these point defects; in their absence, vacancies and interstitials would be distributed more uniformly throughout a wafer. This observation already indicates that the equilibrium concentration of defect depends on the local structure and is not uniquely determined solely by  T  and  V .

Importantly, point defects often evolve further to form defect complexes and secondary defects. It is considered that A-type defects (swirl defects) are formed from interstitials [ 77 ,  78 ] and D-type defects are formed from vacancies [ 79 ]. In addition, the formation of various types of microvoids has been reported during the complicated processes in semiconductor device fabrication [ 80 ,  81 ]. These voids are considered as precipitates of vacancies. In this manner, point defects are often further stabilized through agglomeration. Therefore, it is not possible to define a unique equilibrium configuration of silicon solely by  T  and  V .

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties and Aging
paragraphs: Once the mechanism of strain aging is understood in this manner, it is not surprising to find similar effect in other crystalline materials, regardless of their magnitude, since dislocations and interstitial atoms are common features of crystals. The concept of dislocation does not directly apply to glasses, because the Burgers vector cannot be well defined. However, for metallic glasses, the analogous role is played by the so-called shear transformation zone [ 84 ,  85 ]. Similar mechanisms can reasonably be expected in network glass through analogous structural units, where certain regions exhibit higher local strain than others. Various aging effects have been reported for a wide range of glass materials, depending on the properties being measured [ 86 ,  87 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 ,  91 – 92 ]. Although the author does not claim detailed knowledge of the mechanisms in individual cases, it is certain that they share a common feature: the presence of numerous local minima in the potential energy landscape and the associated relaxation times.

sections.heading: Summary of History-Dependent Phenomena
Approaches from Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
Failure of a Previous Postulate
paragraphs: In this section, the fundamental statement ( 2 ) is derived from the laws of thermodynamics. The definitions of equilibrium and state variable are fundamental issues in thermodynamics. These two problems form a coupled pair. State variables, such as temperature, are quantities that characterize equilibrium, yet they can be defined only after equilibrium itself has been established. This leads to a circular definition, analogous to the chicken-and-egg problem 6 . Let us examine how this issue is treated in the authoritative thermodynamics textbook by Callen [ 52 ]. In sect. 1.5 of his book, this circularity is discussed (Ref. [ 52 ], p. 15). Rather than attempting a derivation, he adopted an approach based on postulations, whose validity is judged by the result that it leads to. He introduces the following postulate:

Callen’s equilibrium postulate :  There exist particular states (called equilibrium states) of simple systems that, macroscopically, are characterized completely by the internal energy  U and the volume V . (Ref. [ 52 ], p. 13)

The original statement of Callen includes additional variables of chemical compositions; however, these are omitted here because chemical reactions are not considered in this paper. Through an appropriate transformation of variables, his statement can be interpreted as asserting that the equilibrium state of a system is uniquely specified by  T  and  V . This is equivalent to the statement of Eq. ( 1 ), and the postulate is indeed valid for gases. Although its applicability to solids is uncertain, Callen implicitly extended it to solids. He was aware of the history-dependent behaviors of solids, such as the hysteresis observed in steel. At this point, two possible interpretations were available: either the postulate is not valid for solids or steel is not an equilibrium material. Callen adopted the latter interpretation. It is unclear whether he regarded steel as a rare case. However, as discussed in Sect.  3 , hysteresis behavior is very common across all solids. Therefore, if Callen’s view is followed, it would imply that all observed states of solids are nonequilibrium states. This is a fundamental dilemma in the thermodynamics of solids, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not yet been satisfactorily resolved.

sections.heading: Structure as a Form of Constraint

paragraphs: One of the most challenging issue in defining equilibrium is the distinction between the absence of change and infinitesimally slow change, which has led to considerable confusion in the thermodynamics literature. Based on observations of aging in glasses, it is often argued that the current state of a glass is undergoing an extremely slow evolution. However, aging is a common phenomenon in solids in general, as already discussed in Sect.  3 . Aging is essentially a manifestation of atom relaxation. (Scherer recommended using the term “structural relaxation" to describe aging [ 116 ]).

In the Gibbs’ era, the nature of passive resistance was not known, because no atomic theory existed. Today, it is recognized that passive resistance arises from energy barrier. From this perspective, the two cases discussed above need not be distinguished: no equilibrium state exists without constraints. In the first case, the presence of a container wall is implicitly assumed in order to specify the volume  V  of the gas. This wall constitutes a constraint. Microscopically, energy barriers within the atomic structure of the metal wall prevent the gas molecules from escaping. In practice, even the robust metal containers cannot maintain their initial pressure for long years. Because the energy barriers have finite heights, gas molecules can diffuse through them, albeit at extremely slow rates. Similarly, in the case of ammonia synthesis, the reaction can proceed over very long time scale. For instance, ammonia has been detected in the solar system, although it is unclear whether this results from long-term relaxation processes or from external events such as high-energy impacts. More generally, any fossil fuel must remain in a stable equilibrium state over its relevant time scale: otherwise it would be consumed before it could be utilized. These considerations indicate that all equilibrium states are sustained by constraints, and that no equilibrium is eternal.

sections.heading: Definition 4.1
Corollary 4.1
Definition 4.2
paragraphs: (Equilibrium) A system is said to be in equilibrium if it is impossible to extract work from it without producing any net effect on the environment. (Ref. [ 51 ], p. 58)

This definition does not invoke state variables. Furthermore, it has the advantage that no information about the internal structure is required; it relies solely on external observable effects. For example, when gas turbulence occurs in a container, work can be extracted from it. Similarly, when a chemical reaction takes place, work can be extracted by inserting a heat engine to convert the released heat into work. If work could be extracted from a system in equilibrium without producing any effect on the environment, the only possible change would be a decrease in the internal energy  U  of the system. This means that work would be obtained solely by cooling the system. This contradicts the Clausius statement of the second law. Therefore, Definition  4.2  admits no exceptions. It is our daily observation that no work can be extracted from glass materials. The only consistent interpretation of this observation is that a glass is in an equilibrium state, provided that its atom configuration remains unchanged.

Reproducibility
paragraphs: Lastly, reproducibility of glass is discussed. History dependence poses challenges for material preparation. If the properties of the target material cannot be reliably reproduced, commercial production becomes difficult. Fortunately, in many cases, experimentalists obtain a high degree of reproducibility even for materials exhibiting history dependence. In today’s commercial productions of memory materials, manufacturers are able to fabricate devices with sufficient accuracy to meet high-quality industrial demands. 8

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The glass state has long been regarded as a nonequilibrium state, because of its history dependence. In this paper, this characterization has been reexamined from the standpoint of fundamentals of thermodynamics. Such a reassessment is necessary because previous arguments often failed to distinguish thermodynamic states from processes, leading to significant conceptual confusions. The central flaw in earlier reasoning is the implicit assumption that  T  and  V  exhaust the set of independent state variables. Although this assumption is valid for gases, its applicability to solids has never been proven and thus has been critically examined here.

The analysis in Sect.  4.2  shows that no material exists in an eternal equilibrium. The notion of equilibrium is therefore meaningful only within the characteristic time, that is, the relaxation time. Various types defect states are created by the preparation conditions of the crystal growth. These defect states are identified by atom configuration  K . All such defect states, which are conventionally regarded as metastable, should instead be considered as equilibrium states within their relaxation times. Conversely, the perfect crystal, which is traditionally regarded as the most stable state, is in fact thermodynamically unstable (see Sect.  3.2 ).
